replying_to: Replying to Training Deep Generative Models via Auxiliary Supervised Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3340 by Reviewer nUPN

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a method for training deep generative models with a latent variable structure by individually training the components (encoder, decoder and prior). The authors frame this as first training an encoder to generate latent samples and then treating training the decoder as a “supervised” learning problem. The authors then introduce a mutual information-based training objective for training the encoder. The authors show reconstructions and samples on Fashion-MNIST and CelebA as well as a few synthetic datasets to support their claims.
content.main_review:
As I mentioned in my summary, it seems to me that, in the VAE-ASL case, this approach simply boils down to training a VAE, then holding the encoder fixed and continuing to train the decoder. Possibly also training a more expressive density for the prior p(z). I honestly don’t find the motivation for this approach convincing. The motivation as described in section 2 comes down to the assertion that supervised learning is inherently easier than unsupervised learning, which is a very broad and not necessarily true claim. The authors don’t really make any theoretical claims about why, all else being equal, this 2-stage process would produce better results. They do state that their approach is meaningful if p(x|u) has small uncertainty, but I don’t see how this changes from standard VAE training. My intuition is that this approach would likely produce worse results, and I’m not sure that the experiments disprove this.

The authors give another motivation in section 4, which is that in typical VAEs the prior and conditional distributions [p(z), p(x|z), q(z|x)] are all assumed to be Gaussian, which can be overly restrictive. Many prior works (which the authors cite) do not make this assumption and allow for training VAEs with more expressive distributions. The authors simply state “they still suffer from the limitations of VAE” without further explanation. They also do not compare against any of these methods in their experiments, so it’s hard to determine if any shown advantages of their model would hold up if the VAEs compared against used more expressive priors/posteriors.

For the MI based method, it seems to me that if the encoder is structured in the same way as the typical VAE, that is $U \sim \sigma_{\phi}(x) \cdot \epsilon + \mu_{\phi}$, then bound in theorem 1 is exactly equivalent to the reconstruction loss of a standard VAE with Gaussian likelihoods: $E_{q(z)}[p(x |z]$. It does seem that the encoder structure could potentially be different here, though it’s implied that the experiments use the standard structure. The regularizer used for U does appear to be meaningfully different, but there is no discussion of why this particular regularizer was chosen. I would like to see this regularization approach compared and contrasted with the the standard VAE’s KL(q(z|x)||p(z)) loss and perhaps discussion if there are differences in the encoders being used. If there is a strong theoretical and empirical argument for this these changes to DGM training I would recommend restructuring the paper to focus on that.

As mentioned above my main issue with the experiments it that this approach is only compared against a standard VAE and not against any more modern improvements to that model. For the synthetic experiments only a 2D latent space is used and the network architectures used are unclear, as is the architecture used for p(u). Based on my experience I would say that existing VAE methods could easily fit those datasets as well as the ASL approach if tuned to the same extent.

The qualitative results look reasonable, on-par with what I would expect from a recent VAE approach, but there is no quantitative comparison on image data. This work would benefit from reporting held out likelihoods or something like FID scores.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I’m unfortunately very skeptical of the claimed benefits of the proposed approach. I feel that this paper needs significantly stronger motivation and greatly expanded experiments with stronger, more contemporary baselines.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

content.title: Clearer explanations on the motivation, and more experiment results
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out some unclear parts of the previous
article, and we hope the resposes below can clarify them.

> *It seems to me that, in the VAE-ASL case, this approach simply boils down to training a VAE, then holding the encoder fixed and continuing to train the decoder... I honestly don’t find the motivation for this approach convincing.*

VAE-ASL and VAE are algorithmically similar, but they are derived from very
different loss functions.

Our main motivation for ASL is that if the encoder is good, then learning
$p(x|u)$ would be a simple task. If both $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$ are accurately
learned, then the resulting estimates for $p(x)$ are also good.

> *The motivation as described in section 2 comes down to the assertion that supervised learning is inherently easier than unsupervised learning, which is a very broad and not necessarily true claim.*

In fact we have mentioned in Section 2.2 that supervised learning is **not** necessarily easier than unsupervised learning. The difficulty of training
depends on the choice of the encoder, and in Section 3 we have provided
conditions on which the learning is easy.

> *The authors don’t really make any theoretical claims about why, all else being equal, this 2-stage process would produce better results... I don’t see how this changes from standard VAE training...*

As mentioned above, it is possible to consistently estimate $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$,
thus resulting in a consistent estimator for $p(x)$. VAE, on the other hand,
does not directly maximizes $p(x)$ but instead a lower bound. In this sense,
the objective function of ASL has the theoretically correct target.

We have added more explanations on the difference between ASL and VAE in
Section 4 of the revised article. As an example, the new MI-based method to
pre-train the encoder is quite different from the standard VAE training.
For the quality of results, we have added experiments on the CIFAR-10 data set,
and have reported the FID scores as an evaluation metric. We do see visible
improvements to VAE-based methods.

> *The authors simply state “they still suffer from the limitations of VAE” without further explanation...*

Thanks for pointing out the problem. We have discussed this topic in Section 4
of the revised article. Our observation is that VAE tries to match $p_xp_{u|x}$
with $p_up_{x|u}$, but this does not imply shared information between $U$ and
$X$. In other words, VAE-based methods do not necessarily generate good latent
representations, which is a limitation of the VAE objective function.

We validate this point in Section 5.2, where we show that VAE-based encoder
does not generate meaningful latent variables, whereas MI-ASL is able to fix
this issue.

The two-stage VAE [1] we compare in the experiments belongs to the class of
methods that use a more expressive prior/posterior, and we see cases where
ASL still gives better results.

> *It seems to me that if the encoder is structured in the same way as the typical VAE, then bound in theorem 1 is exactly equivalent to the reconstruction loss of a standard VAE with Gaussian likelihoods... It’s implied that the experiments use the standard structure.*

The bound is not equivalent to the reconstruction loss in VAE due to the
presence of the denominator $a_i$. For VAE-ASL, the encoder has the same
structure as VAE, but in MI-ASL we use the free form $U=f(X,\varepsilon)$,
which is much more expressive.

> *There is no discussion of why this particular regularizer was chosen...*

The biggest advantage of the proposed regularizer is that it does not require a
tractable density function for $p(u|x)$, so we can use the more expressive form
$U=f(X,\varepsilon)$. The power of this MI-based encoder is illustrated in
Section 5.2, where we see that the VAE-based encoder fails to capture the latent
representation but MI-ASL can.

> *As mentioned above my main issue with the experiments it that this approach is only compared against a standard VAE...*

The baseline model we compare with is two-stage VAE [1], which has been reported
to achieve FID scores comparable to advanced GANs.
Our new experiment results show that under the same network achitecture,
ASL can achieve better scores than two-stage VAE. This implies that ASL
is competitive with modern variants of deep generative models, and almost requires no heavy tuning.

For the 2D synthetic data, all of the networks are Dense networks with three hidden layers, see Appendix A.2.

> *There is no quantitative comparison on image data...*

Thanks for the suggestions. We have added the FID scores in the revised version.

[1] Dai, B., & Wipf, D. (2019). Diagnosing and enhancing VAE models. ICLR 2019 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=B1e0X3C9tQ).

content.title: Response to authors
content.comment:
> Our main motivation for ASL is that if the encoder is good, then learning $p(x|u)$ would be a simple task. If both $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$  are accurately learned, then the resulting estimates for $p(x)$ are also good.

I agree with this statement, but I still don't have any good intuition for why this doesn't also apply to standard VAE training. Intuitively, wouldn't $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$ be easier to optimize if you can also fine tune the encoder at the same time? If not, then why not?

> As mentioned above, it is possible to consistently estimate p(x|u) and p(u), thus resulting in a consistent estimator for p(x). VAE, on the other hand, does not directly maximizes p(x) but instead a lower bound. In this sense, the objective function of ASL has the theoretically correct target.

Strictly speaking, aren't you optimizing $p(x, u)$, where $x$ and $u$ are now both observed? Why is that equivalent to directly optimizing $p(x)$?

> In fact we have mentioned in Section 2.2 that supervised learning is not necessarily easier than unsupervised learning. The difficulty of training depends on the choice of the encoder, and in Section 3 we have provided conditions on which the learning is easy.

The changes do make your claims clearer and more reasonable, however I still have issues with how the motivation is presented in the introduction. It still implies turning this into a supervised task is inherently what makes things easier, but more specifically you claim: "[it] benefits from advances in deep supervised learning and representation learning techniques", but don't give any examples of what these techniques are, why they're helpful for training a decoder here and why they couldn't be applied to end-to-end VAE training. Could you give me some specific examples to convince me that this is really a benefit?

> For the quality of results, we have added experiments on the CIFAR-10 data set, and have reported the FID scores as an evaluation metric. We do see visible improvements to VAE-based methods.

These are great additions, I appreciate the effort put in to running these experiments.

> The bound is not equivalent to the reconstruction loss in VAE due to the presence of the denominator $a_i$. 

But isn't $a_i$ just equivalent to the variance parameter of a Gaussian in this case? I suppose the difference would be that the $a_i$ variables are learned globally rather than as a decoder output, but this has also been explored before: ["Simple and Effective VAE Training with Calibrated Decoders"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13202)

> For VAE-ASL, the encoder has the same structure as VAE, but in MI-ASL we use the free form $U= f(X,\epsilon)$, which is much more expressive... The biggest advantage of the proposed regularizer is that it does not require a tractable density function

It seems you have clarified the actual structure used in your encoder and I see that it's not equivalent to the standard reparameterizable encoder. Thanks for making this change. I would still like to see a controlled comparison between this approach and the more common method of using a normalizing flow to make the distribution of $q(z|x)$ more expressive. 

Again this MI + Stein Discrepency approach seems more interesting to me than the ASL framework, which is why I'd like to see controlled comparisons to it. I'm not clear exactly where the benefits are coming from. How does this method compare without the second-stage tuning of the decoder? Perhaps just training p(u) post-hoc.

> The baseline model we compare with is two-stage VAE [1], which has been reported to achieve FID scores comparable to advanced GANs

This is definitely a good comparison that I didn't appreciate in my first pass. I still think it's necessary to compare to other modern VAEs as mentioned. Do you think your techniques could be extended to state of the art VAEs, such that the NVAE?

content.title: Thanks for the comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the additional references and agree that the article can be improved following the suggestions. Below are some of our further explanations.

> I agree with this statement, but I still don't have any good intuition for why this doesn't also apply to standard VAE training. Intuitively, wouldn't $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$ be easier to optimize if you can also fine tune the encoder at the same time? If not, then why not?

Indeed VAE jointly tunes the encoder and decoder at the same time, but its target is not the true likelihood function but a lower bound. This gap may drive $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$ to a sub-optimal solution. 

> Strictly speaking, aren't you optimizing $p(x,u)$, where $x$ and $u$ are now both observed? Why is that equivalent to directly optimizing $p(x)$?

Since the joint distribution determines the marginal distribution, learning $p(x,u)$ accurately implies a good estimator for $p(x)$.

> Could you give me some specific examples to convince me that this is really a benefit?

The mutual information criterion is one such example, which has attracted many attentions in recent representation learning literature.

replying_to: Replying to Training Deep Generative Models via Auxiliary Supervised Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3340 by Reviewer 6DAm

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new way to train deep generative models by framing the learning problem as a supervised learning algorithm.

Since p(x,u) = p(u|x)p(x), they first pretrain an encoder p(u|x), then draw a dataset (u,x) with x ~ p(x) and u ~ p(u|x), then learn an unconditional model p(u) and a regression model p(x|u).
content.main_review:
Overall, I like the idea proposed in this paper. However my review changed significantly (from an accept to a reject) once I have seen the experimental section, which I don't find enough. This is the main weakness in the paper, and I provide the reasons later in this review.

First, some comments. I think introduction should cite diffusion probabilistic generative models and autoregressive models, which are the other main family of deep generative models (first paragraph in the introduction).

I find section 2.2 incorrect. I don't agree with the fact that in a supervised learning algorithm  we assume that p(y|x) is concentrated around its mean value, and that the standard deviation is unwanted. This has to do, with the fact, that usual training criteria such as L_2 norm assumes p(y|x) is Gaussian, and optimal Bayes decision theory tell us that we should predict the mean (when we use an L2 loss function in our Bayes rule) in order to minimize the error probability. But in my opinion this is not something inherited form the supervised learning algorithm but from the decision we want to make with our trained model. Actually, one is free to learn the conditional variance from p(y|x,sigma) as practitioners do, for example, with Gaussian processes. So in general I think that the paper claim:  "Therefore, the ASL framework is meaningful when the conditional distribution px|u(x|u) has a small uncertainty.", should be justified in another way. Actually I dont understand what the authors want to tell us here. I recommend clarifying this point.

Another thing I think the authors should somehow motivate/clarify is related to section 3.1. The authors claim (based on a reference) that a VAE with latent_space > observed_space  can optimally reconstruct X. However, earlier in the manuscript they motivate the need of observed_space >> latent_space so that the density estimation of p(u) is easier. So I dont really see the point of section 3.1 Perhaps the authors should use a VAE with latent_space <<< observed_space and use a normalizing flow to enhance the representation power of q(z|u) in order to obtain a more optimal VAE for their comparison

I think there is an error in figure 5. Isnt the figure of the middle the figure MI-ASL rather than VAE-ASL? I find the figures from the middle sharper.

I think the experiments are not enough. I think that to provide more light into the framework some likelihood values should be provided on a test set, and compare with other deep generative models where likelihoods can be estimated such as: VAE ,normalizing flows or autoregressive models.  And also perhaps adding one or two more datasets such as CIFAR10. Also I think it will be meaningful to compare the likelihoods assigned to out of distribution samples with other models so that we can also see how this new deep generative framework do on this task.

Note that I dont really expect the framework to be better just to be accepted for this conference. I like the idea so I am just asking to see at which point is this new deep generative framework in comparison to others. I think this is an important point to set the base for future research on this family of generative models. Hence I cannot recommend accepting the paper in its current form. If all my concerns are addressed I'd change my score to an accept. Unfortunately, I think there is no time enough to complete all the things I'd expect to see.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- Some small issues to correct 
- Experimental evaluation is clearly missing important points to provide light into the proposed approach.

content.title: Crucial clarifications and improved experiments
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for pointing out some claims in the previous
version that may cause confusions. The article has been rephrased for better
clarity.

> *I think introduction should cite diffusion probabilistic generative models and autoregressive models, which are the other main family of deep generative models (first paragraph in the introduction).*

Thanks for the suggestions. We have cited these models in our introduction part.

> *I don't agree with the fact that in a supervised learning algorithm we assume that p(y|x) is concentrated around its mean value, and that the standard deviation is unwanted.*

We thank the reviewer to point out this ambiguity in the previous version.
What we really want to convey is that by choosing a proper encoder $p(u|x)$,
$p(x|u)$ can be easily estimated by supervised learning algorithms.
In **one** special case that $p(x|u)$ is almost determined by the
conditional mean, learning $p(x|u)$ reduces to learning the regression
function, which is a relatively simple task. There are, of course,
**other** cases where $p(x|u)$ is not a degenerate distribution but
can also be learned. What we show in the article is one possible scenario,
but it does not apply to all supervised learning tasks.

We have rephrased the article to better express our thoughts.
In the new version, we show in Section 2.2 that supervised learning can be
hard, and in Section 3 we give conditions on which learning $p(x|u)$ is easy.

> *The authors claim (based on a reference) that a VAE with latent_space > observed_space can optimally reconstruct X.*

First we would like to clarify that it is not the dimension of the observed
space, but the intrinsic dimension of the manifold. For the notation, $p$
stands for the ambient dimension of the data, $d$ is the intrinsic
dimension, typically with $d\ll p$, and $r$ is the latent dimension we
choose. Therefore, what we really claim in the article is that a VAE with
latent_space ($r$) > intrinsic_manifold ($d$) can reconstruct $X$.

> *I dont really see the point of section 3.1.*

The purpose of Section 3.1 is to give one possible method to obtain the
encoder $p(u|x)$ that is needed by ASL. It shows that under some assumptions,
the encoder from a vanilla VAE suffices. But in the more general case,
we advocate the MI-based encoder.

> *I think there is an error in figure 5. Isnt the figure of the middle the figure MI-ASL rather than VAE-ASL? I find the figures from the middle sharper.*

The order of the figures is correct. We find that the figure produced by
MI-ASL shows more details, for example the patterns on the shirts.

> *I think the experiments are not enough.*

Thanks for the suggestions. Since evaluating likelihood values in high
dimensions is not very reliable (in many cases they are only lower bounds), we finally choose FID scores for
quantitative evaluation. We have also added the CIFAR-10 experiments,
and the results are reported in Table 1 in the revised article.

The baseline model we compare with is two-stage VAE [1], which has been reported
to achieve FID scores comparable to advanced GANs.
Our new experiment results show that under the same network achitecture,
ASL can achieve better scores than two-stage VAE. This implies that ASL
is competitive with modern variants of deep generative models, and almost requires no heavy tuning.

[1] Dai, B., & Wipf, D. (2019). Diagnosing and enhancing VAE models. ICLR 2019 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=B1e0X3C9tQ).

replying_to: Replying to Training Deep Generative Models via Auxiliary Supervised Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3340 by Reviewer QNg7

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper takes on the problem of training deep generative models, building on the probabilistic framework of variational autoencoders (VAEs, Kingma & Welling '14). That is, given a large high-dimensional dataset of feature vectors x and a desired latent variable model with low-dimensional encoding variable u, the problem is to produce an "encoder" and "decoder", which allow generating samples or reconstructions and (potentially) computing likelihoods for given features.

Classically, the VAE trains the encoder and decoder simultaneously to maximize a lower bound on the log-likelihood of the data under a latent variable model that assumes Gaussian noise. The claim in this paper seems to be that even though the VAE allows very flexible mean functions in the generative model via neural nets, the Gaussian noise assumption may be too limiting.

To overcome the weaknesses of VAEs, the paper suggests a two-stage process called Auxiliary Supervised Learning (ASL) to fit a deep generative model.

Step 1: Train an "encoder" and a "decoder", using any desired objective, such as:

- maximize ELBO (like a classic VAE)
- maximize a new unbiased bound on Mutual Information (MI, see Sec. 3.2)

Stage 2: Freeze the pretrained encoder from step 1 -- which defines p(u|x) -- and then use samples from this encoder to produce refined models for p(u) and p(x|u) the decoder. In stage 2, the two models can be updated separately in parallel, because given an encoder, each update is decoupled from the other.

The models for p(u) and p(x|u) in this second stage are flexible:
- Marginal density estimation for p(u) can be done via a normalizing flow or other sample-then-transform explicit likelihood model
- Conditional density estimation for p(x|u) -- called "supervised learning" in the paper -- could also use a flexible model, but for experiments it seems the probabilistic model chosen is like a classic VAE decoder with mean determined by a neural network and Gaussian noise.

Experiments examine the visual quality of generative samples and reconstructions, compared to classic VAEs and to normalizing flows.
content.main_review:
# Strengths

+ The new bound on mutual information (MI) that can be used to train probabilistic encoders and decoders is potentially interesting and broadly useful
+ Toy dataset experiments are nice for building some intuition


# Weaknesses

- W0: Clarification / ablation studies needed to understand the value of stage 2
- W1: Conceptual justification of why the second stage procedure is valuable is missing
- W2: Need to cite related work on improving VAE optimization of encoder/decoder

## W0: Clarifications and ablations needed to understand the value of stage 2

Stage 1 (VAE or MI) produces an encoder and a decoder, as well as an initial marginal p(u).
Stage 2 (ASL) produces a latent variable marginal p(u) and a refined decoder p(x|u).

I think readers would benefit from knowing which products from each stage are used in each experimental result. For example, to make a "reconstruction" (as in Fig 5), I think you need the new decoder but not the marginal p(u).... is that right? Because you are given the image x, and you just sample from the encoder and then from the decoder.

I suggest in each figure/caption, you point out exactly how the result benefits from the ASL procedure (does it use the new p(u)? does it use the new p(x|u)?)

I also suggest you consider making side-by-side plots that show various "ablations", such as:

- Showing a result from using the MI objective in stage 1, without ASL stage 2
- Keeping the marginal from stage 1 fixed, and showing a result with stage 1 and stage 2 decoders
- Compute the training-set ELBO using the encoder from stage 1, and the decoders from stage 1 (classic VAE) and from stage 2 (your VAE+ASL). This will suggest if stage 1 optimization is delivering the best possible solution (I hypothesize it is not, see W1 and W2 below).

Without these clarifications, it is difficult to understand why some results look better than others.
I particularly wonder if the MI objective alone might somehow produce good results without the need for further ASL refinement.



## W1: Conceptual justification for the second stage is inadequate : Is the improvement from Representation, Objective, or Algorithm?

Why should we expect that given a fixed encoder (which essentially freezes the joint distribution p(x,u) you are trying to model), that the second stage refinement of the decoder p(x|u) should produce a better model than the original decoder training process?

From what I can tell, the decoder used here is still using Gaussian noise and the same architecture as in stage 1. Thus, the representations used here are the same as in stage 1, and if the new decoder is "better" after stage 2, shouldn't the decoder produced by stage two also be considered better under the original objective used to pretrain in stage 1?

My hypothesis is that, if you use a classic VAE in stage 1 and then refine as proposed in this paper in stage 2, that the improvements seen in the experiments are really just due to the fact that the stage 1 optimization is notoriously bad at producing high-quality decoder/encoders (see W2 below for literature). Thus, if you had a better algorithm for stage 1 (or simply just ran stage 1 longer to get better convergence), I suspect you'd get similar gains to your ASL-VAE.

In the rebuttal, I hope the authors can clarify: Is the improvement from a new representation/model? Or do you agree with my understanding that we're really just overcoming an algorithmic deficiency from stage 1 (the stage 1 objective is good, but the algorithm cannot find great solutions)?


## W2: Missing connections to previous literature on improving VAE encoder/decoder optimization

There is substantial literature that suggests that the usual simultaneous gradient-based training of both the encoder and decoder in VAEs has problems due to the two models falling out of "sync" (the encoder is not a good approximation of the posterior implied by the decoder, or vice versa). As a remedy, the literature suggests that interleaving different updates or subtly adjusting the objective during training can somewhat fix the poor performance of the resulting encoder/decoder.

For example, see the studies

- Lagging Inference Networks and Posterior Collapse in Variational Autoencoders (He et al. ICLR 2019)
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.05534.pdf

- Semi-Amortized Variational Autoencoders (Kim et al. ICML 2018)
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.02550.pdf

- Cyclical Annealing Schedule: A Simple Approach to Mitigating KL Vanishing (Fu et al. NAACL 2019)
https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10145

Like the present work, these works alternatively freeze one part (encoder or decoder) and update the other, or otherwise interleave standard joint gradient updates with other updates. Substantial gains in VAE solution quality result, because the optimization algorithm is better at finding solutions (using the original standard VAE objective).

I'd like the authors to comment on how they see their proposed method (which freezes the encoder and only refines the decoder) as compared to these ideas (which perform more extensive algorithmic adjustments).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the paper has some interesting insights (especially the new lower bound on the Mutual Information, which could be a contribution on its own if properly elaborated). However, I don't think the paper adequately explains the value of the "stage two" ASL procedure (the refinement of p(u) and p(x|u) given a fixed encoder). I have concerns about both the conceptual justification and the experimental justification of stage two, and I think there are missing connections to the growing literature on improving optimization of VAEs that would be essential before a version should be accepted.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

display_title: Important clarifications on the stage 1 and stage 2 of ASL

content.title: Important clarifications on the stage 1 and stage 2 of ASL
content.comment:
Thanks for the detailed and constructive comments. We would like to first make
one clarification on the "stage 1" of ASL, as both W0 and W1 are dependent on
this.

Technically speaking, stage 1 only involves the encoder and is not about the
decoder. For example, in the MI-based method, mutual information and the
regularizer are functions only of the encoder. But to estimate MI, we need
an auxiliary function $g$, which happens to have the same structure as the
decoder. The optimal $g$ for objective function (3) does not mean that it is
a good decoder, since we have a separate loss function for $g$ (the supervised
learning). In Section 3.3, we also mention a few methods that can learn the
encoder without introducing g.

Making this clear, the value of stage 2 is then obvious. It defines the optimal
values of the decoder based on supervised learning, and also learns the prior
$p(u)$. Conceptually, given the encoder obtained in stage 1, the decoder
can be learned purely from scratch. VAE-ASL and MI-ASL simplify this part
because they provide warm starts for the decoder, thus giving an illusion
of the fine-tuning step. In the ASL framework, fine-tuning is in the
implementation level, not in the methodology level.

**W0**: We think a sensible ablation is on the encoders. Given an encoder,
we train $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$ to the optimum, so the difference comes from the
choice of the encoder. Figure 4 and Figure 5 then show the difference between
VAE-ASL and MI-ASL: the MI-based encoder indeed has better latent representation
and smaller reconstruction error.

**W1**: In Section 4 of the revised article, we point out two factors that may
explain the improvements. First, vanilla VAE puts restrictions on
the prior and posterior, whereas ASL allows richer classes for both. Second,
even though there are various works allowing more expressive priors and
posteriors, the objective function of VAE also has limitations: VAE does
not necessarily produce meaningful latent representations, but this is also
an important task of generative modeling.

In contrast, our main motivation for ASL is that if the encoder is good, then
learning $p(x|u)$ would be a simple task. Therefore, it is possible to
consistently estimate $p(x|u)$ and $p(u)$, thus resulting in a consistent estimator for $p(x)$. Also, the explicit optimization on MI makes the encoder
more likely to generate meaningful latent representations.

**W2**: We thank the reviewer for providing these references, and we have
added them in the related work. We appreciate the ideas and works that improve
the optimization process of VAE, but as we have mentioned above, one unique
value of ASL is that it does not rely on the objective function of VAE,
thus making it possible to overcome the intrinsic limitation of VAE on
representation learning.

content.title: Further suggestions for ablations / deeper discussion of related work needed
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for engaging with my feedback. I continue to think additional ablations and deeper discussion of related work is necessary.

### RE what happens in "stage 1" and W0

The response above writes "Technically speaking, stage 1 only involves the encoder and is not about the decoder."
I agree that in general that, if someone developed an encoder p(u|x), then the proposed ASL method could apply to this encoder.

However, *in practice*, there are two ways this present work is operationalized:
- VAE-ASL, in which a decoder is trained simultaneously with the encoder
- MI-ASL, which relies on a function g, whose most natural interpretation from Eq 3 is definitely as a decoder (I read Eq 3 as minimizing reconstruction error between observed X and reconstruction g(u) )

Thus, in some sense the decoder from stage 1 is already there waiting for us. Shouldn't we make sure this decoder doesn't suffice, before we go to additional expense to refine it via ASL?

Bottom line: I think it is essential that additional ablation experiments convince the reader that:
- (1) the decoder from the ASL part of the method is convincingly better than decoders from earlier parts of the pipeline
- (2) whether the new marginal p(u) is essential, or whether it is the new decoder only that is better
- (3) whether the overall improved encoder-decoder pair for any VAE-ASL method would have been preferred by the VAE baseline if optimization issues didn't get in the way

### RE W2: Suggested references on "lagging" inference networks

I think the current revision is inadequate. The current text reads: "there are various works on improving
the optimization process of VAE (Kim et al 2018, He et al 2019, Fu et al 2019)"

This phrase makes it seem like these papers are distantly related to the present work.

In my view, at least He et al is a closely related work that suggests a different and insightful hypothesis for why the VAE-ASL results in this paper are better than the plain VAE baseline (because plain VAEs have "lagging" between encoders and decoders when trained simultaneously, leading to suboptimal results).

display_title: Official Review of Paper3340 by Reviewer chEF

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an alternative approach to training deep latent generative models, named Auxiliary Supervised Learning (ASL). The authors make use of the obvious fact that if the latent representations are given (via some pre-trained encoder) then learning the generative model becomes a much easier task; $\max \log p(x_n,z_n) \ \text{for }n = 1 \cdots N$. In other words, the unsupervised learning problem which involves a difficult integral is transformed into a supervised learning problem. To train the distribution $p(z)$, the authors propose to use a flow. With regards to how to obtain the encoder to generate the latent representations $z$, the authors discuss various approaches including a new approach which is obtained by optimizing a (novel to the best of my knowledge) bound on $I(x,z)$. The authors then perform some experiments on toy-datasets as well as FashinMNIST and CIFAR-10 in order to demonstrate that the new model is able to generate samples with reasonable quality.
content.main_review:
**General Comment**	

While I beleive researching new methods to train deep latent generative models to be very important and of interest to the ICLR community, I am not sure the current draft meets the bar of an ICLR submission. What I see the major problems with this paper are the following:

- It seems to me that this paper reverses the problem of representation learning via deep generative models. Many of the common use cases of deep generative models are in fact *not*  generation, but focused on the representation learning aspect (e.g. the literature on disengagement. topic modelling, clustering, scene understating, ….). And one of the main reasons we train generative models is with the hope that the posterior of the learned model represents meaningful features about the data and has a good notion of uncertainty. The current paper is trying to solve the inverse problem which is: if we already have good features, can we train a good generative model. I am not necessarily saying this problem does not make sense, however, it should be mentioned that this drops many of the use cases for why people use models such as VAEs. In fact, the part I enjoyed most about the paper was Section 3.2 which discusses a new approach to learn representations via MI maximization. I am not very familiar with the MI estimation. Assuming that the proposed model in Section 3.2 is novel, I would rewrite the paper around Eq.3, but that requires another revision. 
- Even solely focusing on generation, I don’t see this approach competing with other generative models such as GANs or flows, given the likelihood is still defined at a pixel-level. The only VAE based approaches that are able to compete in terms of generation are hierarchical VAEs such as NVAE which has many layers of latent representations and I do not see an easy way of extending the proposed approach to hierarchical generative models. 
- With regards to novelty, I find this paper more of a *framing* of existing objectives rather than a new model. For example, the log-likelihood $\mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)]$ in VAE can also be interpreted as a supervised task where $z$ is generated from the encoder. In other words, how much ASL is different from a VAE that is trained by first training the encoder fully and then the decoder? I understand the prior on $u$ here is a flow but this prior has also been used in VAEs as well [1].
- In my opinion, the experiments do not show enough evidence that there is much gain. There is no quantitative comparison in terms of generation. It is hard to tell for me from Fig 6, if the 2-stage VAE is any worse than ASL. And the baselines here are mostly very simple.

**Clarity**

The paper is very well-written. Good job!

**Questions**

- Could the authors expand on the choice of $u \sim f(x,\epsilon)$? Why not simply use a re-parameterized Gaussian? How much would this matter? Sorry if I missed this in the paper. 
- Is there a particular reason for why the notation was changed from $z$ to $u$ for the latent representations? 


**References**

[1] Bauer, Matthias, and Andriy Mnih. "Resampled priors for variational autoencoders." The 22nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2019.

display_title: ASL targets on both good representation and generation

content.title: ASL targets on both good representation and generation
content.comment:
First we would thank the reviewer for the various helpful comments.
We have made improvements to the article and hope the responses below
explain the confusions in the previous version.

> (*Reversing the problem of representation learning*)

We are glad to see that the reviewer raised this interesting question.
In fact, we also share the similar point of view that learning the latent
representation is an important part of deep generative models. However,
as we have demonstrated in Figure 4, existing deep generative models does
not necessarily generate good latent representations. The current paper
advocates the insight that if we can get a good encoder/representation,
then good generation is also achieveable, and we have provided concrete
schemes (Section 3) to find such encoders. In this sense, ASL is one
framework that targets on **both** good representation and good generation.

> *Even solely focusing on generation, I don’t see this approach competing with other generative models such as GANs or flows, given the likelihood is still defined at a pixel-level. The only VAE based approaches that are able to compete in terms of generation are hierarchical VAEs such as NVAE which has many layers of latent representations and I do not see an easy way of extending the proposed approach to hierarchical generative models.*

As we have mentioned above, we care about both generation and representation.
Compared with GAN, ASL takes advantage of encoders and we could find the latent representations of data, which is a very important task for generative models. For flows, they do not allow a low-dimensional latent space, thus encountering difficulties with high-dimensional data.

In terms of the quality of generation, we have added experiments on the
CIFAR-10 data set, and have reported evaluation metrics such as the
FID scores. The method to compare with is the two-stage VAE [1], which
has been reported to achieve FID scores comparable to GANs.
Our new experiment results show that under the same network achitecture,
ASL can achieve better scores than two-stage VAE. This implies that ASL
is competitive with modern variants of deep generative models, and almost requires no heavy tuning.

> *With regards to novelty, I find this paper more of a framing of existing objectives rather than a new model.*

We think our novelty is two-fold. First, it provides new insights on the
training of deep generative models beyond the framework of VAE. It explicitly
puts an emphasis on the quality of representation learning, which is not
necessarily true in VAE-based methods. Second, we propose a new method to
learn the encoder, which is quite different from the VAE framework. In fact,
we have shown in Secion 5.2 that it is superior to VAE in the representation
learning task.

> *For example, the log-likelihood in VAE can also be interpreted as a supervised task where z is generated from the encoder.*

There is indeed a term in the loss function of VAE that is similar to supervised learning, but it is not the actual objective function. In
contrast, in ASL we explicitly forms a supervised learning task.

> *In other words, how much ASL is different from a VAE that is trained by first training the encoder fully and then the decoder?*

We would say that VAE is **one** method to obtain the encoder. However, as
explained in Section 3.1, its quality relies on some strong assumptions.
We claim that there are **other** methods to learn the encoder beyond
the scope of VAE, and the MI-based method is one such example.
Overall, ASL uses different objectives to train deep
generative models, and has demonstrated great extensibility.


> *In my opinion, the experiments do not show enough evidence that there is much gain. There is no quantitative comparison in terms of generation. It is hard to tell for me from Fig 6, if the 2-stage VAE is any worse than ASL. And the baselines here are mostly very simple.*

Thanks for the suggestions. We have added the CIFAR-10 experiments and
FID scores for quantitative evaluation.

> *Could the authors expand on the choice of $u\sim f(x,\epsilon)$? Why not simply use a re-parameterized Gaussian? How much would this matter? Sorry if I missed this in the paper.*

This is in fact another big advantage of the MI-based encoder, since it does
not require a tractable density function. The form $U=f(X,\epsilon)$ can
almost represent any conditional distribution $p(u|x)$, as long as $f$ is
sufficiently expressive. The Gaussian encoder in VAE may be restrictive.

> *Is there a particular reason for why the notation was changed from $z$ to $u$ for the latent representations?*

We use $z$ to represent the true generating variable, whereas $u$ is
arbitrary and chosen by the user.

[1] Dai, B., & Wipf, D. (2019). Diagnosing and enhancing VAE models. ICLR 2019 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=B1e0X3C9tQ).

content.title: Respond to Authros
content.comment:
Thank you for engaging my review,

I have read the authors response and other reviews. I agree with many of the comments from Reviewer QNg7 & 6DAm, particularly regarding W1 and W2 for reviewer QNg7.

I still stand with with my main concern regarding the proposed method. This frameworks drops many of the use case of learning deep generative models (learning $p_\theta(x)$ and inferring $z \sim p_{\theta}(z|x)$) because the representation learning has to be done before training the deep generative model. To be more clear, the representations do *not* necessarily respond to the posterior $p_{\theta}(z|x)$ because we learned the $z$s before learning $\theta$. I do not disagree with the claim that generative models do not necessarily produce good representations. However (1) the representation in generative models at least probably make sense as they are samples from the posterior $p_{\theta}(z|x)$, and (2) What representations we learn heavily depends on the type of inductive bias we use in the VAE (see [1,2] as examples). 

With regards to Figure 4: I am abit suspicions of the results shown in Figure 4. Looking at the appendix, it seems to suggest that the dimension in VAE is only 2 while it is 32 for the MI-based encoder. This makes a big difference. I have trained VAEs on F-MNIST before, and have visualized the latent space. The latent space should not look like that if you use higher dimensions for latent space, at least if you use UMAP to visualize the latent space instead of T-SNE. 

As I mentioned before, I think the new MI-based encoder can be a valuable contribution, and I think it might be a good paper if it is centered around this contribution. However, this requires another submission. 

*Reparametrized Gaussian instead of* $u \sim f(x,\epsilon)$

I understand that $f(x,\epsilon)$ can be more expressive. I guess my question was more to regarding how much improvements we would really gain by changing $f$ to be more flexible empirically.  

*z & u notation*

Thank you for the clarification.

[1] Jiang, Zhuxi, et al. "Variational deep embedding: An unsupervised and generative approach to clustering." arXiv preprint arXiv:1611.05148 (2016).
[2] Lin, Zhixuan, et al. "Space: Unsupervised object-oriented scene representation via spatial attention and decomposition." arXiv preprint arXiv:2001.02407 (2020).

content.title: Thanks for the comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and agree that the article can be improved following these directions.

Regarding Figure 4, we shall clarify that both VAE-ASL and MI-ASL use 32 latent dimensions, and we visualize both of them by projecting to the 2D plane. In fact, if only two latent dimensions are used, then VAE-ASL has a nice clustering structure. We conjecture that it is because in higher dimensions, points are generally distant from each other, so they are not easily clustered based on pairwise distances.
